### 🛠️ Practical Scenario – Automatic Birthday Email Automation

Imagine an organization wants to send birthday greeting emails to its customers automatically.

Instead of manually checking Contact records every day, we will create a Schedule-Triggered Flow that runs daily at 12:00 AM.

Our automation will:

1. Run automatically every day using Schedule-Triggered Flow.
2. Retrieve eligible Contact records using the Contact object as the starting object.
3. Check whether the Contact's Birthdate field is populated.
4. Compare the Contact's birth month and day with the current date using a Formula Resource.
5. Use a Decision element to identify Contacts whose birthday is today.
6. Send a personalized birthday greeting email using the Send Email action.

By the end of this practical, you will understand how to build a daily scheduled automation in Salesforce without writing Apex code.

In this episode, we're going to understand the different types of Salesforce Flow and learn when to use each Flow type.

If you're new to Salesforce Flow, understanding Flow types is one of the first important steps. Before building an automation, you need to understand what should start the Flow and what type of Flow is appropriate for your requirement.

📚 5 Salesforce Flow Types Covered

1️⃣ Record-Triggered Flow

A Record-Triggered Flow starts automatically when a Salesforce record is created, updated, or deleted, depending on the configuration.

Example:
When an Opportunity becomes Closed Won, automatically create a follow-up Task.

2️⃣ Screen Flow

A Screen Flow allows users to interact with a Flow through screens and forms.

Example:
Create an Employee Leave Request form where the employee enters the leave type, dates, and reason.

3️⃣ Autolaunched Flow

An Autolaunched Flow runs in the background without displaying screens to the user and can be invoked by supported automation or processes.

Example:
Create a reusable Flow that calculates a customer's discount and returns the result to another process.

4️⃣ Schedule-Triggered Flow

A Schedule-Triggered Flow starts based on a configured schedule.

Example:
Every night, find Opportunities that haven't been updated for 30 days and create follow-up Tasks.

5️⃣ Platform Event-Triggered Flow

A Platform Event-Triggered Flow starts when Salesforce receives a specific Platform Event.

Example:
An external system publishes a Payment Completed event, and Salesforce uses the Flow to update related records.

🧠 Easy Way to Remember Salesforce Flow Types

Record-Triggered
→ Record changes → Flow starts

Screen Flow
→ User interacts → Flow starts

Autolaunched Flow
→ Another process invokes → Flow starts

Schedule-Triggered Flow
→ Schedule occurs → Flow starts

Platform Event-Triggered Flow
→ Platform Event received → Flow starts

The key question to ask when choosing a Flow type is:

"What should start my Flow?"

Once you understand that, choosing the appropriate Flow type becomes much easier.

🏗️ Salesforce Security Model

We'll understand the four major levels of Salesforce data security:

1️⃣ Organization Level
Controls access to the Salesforce org, including login policies, password policies, login hours, locations, and authentication-related controls.

2️⃣ Object Level
Controls whether a user can access an object and what they can do with its records, such as:

Read
Create
Edit
Delete

3️⃣ Field Level
Controls which individual fields a user can see or edit.

For example, a user may have access to an Employee object but may not be allowed to see sensitive fields such as Salary or Bank Account.

4️⃣ Record Level
Controls which individual records a user can access.

We'll also introduce concepts such as:

These concepts will be covered in greater detail in upcoming Salesforce Admin lessons.

🔑 Authentication vs Authorization

To understand the concept practically, we'll build a real-world Employee Leave Approval Process in Salesforce.

⬇️

Submit for Approval

⬇️

⬇️

Manager Receives Approval Request

⬇️

⬇️

⬇️

This allows Salesforce to automate a business approval workflow without requiring users to manage every step manually.

🧩 Important Approval Process Components

We'll also understand the major components of an Approval Process:

Entry Criteria → Determines which records can enter the approval process.

Approval Steps → Defines who needs to approve the record.

Approver → The user responsible for reviewing the request.

Initial Submission Actions → Actions performed when the record is submitted.

Final Approval Actions → Actions performed when the record is approved.

Final Rejection Actions → Actions performed when the record is rejected.

Recall Actions → Actions performed when an approval request is recalled.

If the manager rejects:

Status → Rejected

Salesforce can also lock and unlock the record and send notifications automatically.

🔒 Record Locking in Approval Processes

You'll also learn why Salesforce can lock a record while it's waiting for approval.

This prevents users from modifying important information while an approver is reviewing the request.

Once the approval process is completed, configured actions can unlock the record.
